The '''Becker–Morduchow–Libby solution''' is a mathematical description of how the properties of a gas—such as pressure, temperature, and density—change within a one-dimensional [[shock wave]]. It is an exact solution of the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] for a compressible, viscous, heat-conducting gas. First derived in a simplified form by German physicist [[Richard Becker (physicist)|Richard Becker]] in 1922, it was later extended by Morris Morduchow and [[Paul A. Libby]] in 1949.<ref>Becker, R. (1922). Stosswelle und detonation. Zeitschrift für Physik, 8(1), 321-362.</ref><ref>Morduchow, M., & Libby, P. A. (1949). On a complete solution of the one-dimensional flow equations of a viscous, heat-conducting, compressible gas. Journal of the Aeronautical Sciences, 16(11), 674-684.</ref> Independent versions were also found in 1944 by M. Roy and L. H. Thomas.<ref>Roy, M., Compt. Rend. Acad. Sci., 218, 813 (1944)</ref><ref>Thomas, L. H., Jour. Chem. Phys., 12, 449 (1944)</ref> The solution revealed an unexpected feature: the [[entropy]] of the gas can vary in a non-monotonic way across the shock, rather than increasing steadily. Earlier work by [[Lord Rayleigh]] and [[G. I. Taylor]] had addressed special cases, such as flows with viscosity but no [[Thermal conduction|heat conduction]], or vice versa.<ref name="rayleigh">Rayleigh, L. (1910). Aerial plane waves of finite amplitude. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character, 84(570), 247-284.</ref><ref name="taylor">Taylor, G. I. (1910). The conditions necessary for discontinuous motion in gases. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character, 84(571), 371-377.</ref><ref>Taylor, G. I., & Maccoll, J. W. (1935). The mechanics of compressible fluids. Durand, Aerodynamic theory, 3.</ref>

==Mathematical description==
In a frame fixed with a planar shock wave, the shock wave is steady. In this frame, the steady [[Navier–Stokes equations]] for a viscous and heat conducting gas can be written as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dx}(\rho u) &= 0,\\
\rho u \frac{du}{dx} + \frac{dp}{dx} - \frac{4}{3}\frac{d}{dx}\left(\mu'\frac{du}{dx}\right) &= 0,\\
\rho u \frac{d\varepsilon}{dx} + p\frac{du}{dx} - \frac{d}{dx}\left(\lambda\frac{dT}{dx}\right) - \frac{4}{3}\mu' \left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2&=0,
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>\rho</math> is the [[density]], <math>u</math> is the velocity, <math>p</math> is the [[pressure]], <math>\varepsilon</math> is the [[internal energy]] per unit mass, <math>T</math> is the temperature, <math>\mu'=\mu+3\zeta/4</math> is an effective coefficient of viscosity, <math>\mu</math> is the [[coefficient of viscosity]], <math>\zeta</math> is the [[second viscosity]] and <math>\lambda</math> is the [[thermal conductivity]]. To this set of equations, one has to prescribe an equation of state <math>f(p,\rho,T)=0</math> and an expression for the energy in terms of any two thermodynamics variables, say <math>\varepsilon=\varepsilon(p,\rho)</math>. Instead of <math>\varepsilon</math>, it is convenient to work with the [[specific enthalpy]] <math>h=\varepsilon + p/\rho.</math>

Let us denote properties pertaining upstream of the shock with the subscript "<math>0</math>" and downstream with "<math>1</math>". The shock wave speed itself is denoted by <math>D=u_0</math>. The first integral of the governing equations, after imposing the condition that all gradients vanish upstream, are found to be
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\rho u &= \rho_0 D,\\
p + \rho u^2 - \frac{4}{3}\mu' \frac{du}{dx} &= p_0 +\rho_0 D^2,\\
h + \frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{1}{\rho_0 D} \left(\lambda \frac{dT}{dx} + \frac{4}{3} \mu' u \frac{du}{dx}\right)&=h_0 +\frac{D^2}{2}.
\end{align}
</math>

By evaluating these on the downstream side where all gradients vanish, one recovers the familiar [[Rankine–Hugoniot conditions]], <math>\rho_1u_1=\rho_0 D</math>, <math>p_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2=p_0+\rho_0 D^2</math> and <math>h_1+u_1^2/2 = h_0 + D^2/2.</math> Further integration of the above equations require numerical computations, except in one special case where integration can be carried out analytically.

===Analytical solution===
[[File:Becker–Morduchow–Libby solution.jpg|thumb|300px|Becker–Morduchow–Libby solution]]
Two assumptions has to be made to facilitate explicit integration of the third equation. First, assume that the gas is [[ideal gas|ideal]] ([[Polytropic gas|polytropic]] since we shall assume constant values for the [[specific heats]]) in which case the equation of state is <math>p/\rho T = c_p(\gamma-1)/\gamma</math> and further <math>h=c_pT</math>, where <math>c_p</math> is the specific heat at constant pressure and <math>\gamma</math> is the [[specific heat ratio]]. The third equation then becomes

<math display="block">h + \frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{4\mu'}{3\rho_0 D} \left( \frac{3}{4Pr'}\frac{dh}{dx} + \frac{1}{2}  \frac{du^2}{dx}\right) = h_0 +\frac{D^2}{2}</math>

where <math>Pr'=\mu'c_p/\lambda</math> is the Prandtl number based on <math>\mu'</math>; when <math>\zeta=0</math>, say as in monoatomic gases, this Prandtl number is just the ordinary [[Prandtl number]] <math>Pr=\mu c_p/\lambda</math>. The second assumption made is <math>Pr'=3/4</math> so that the terms inside the parenthesis becomes a [[total derivative]], i.e., <math>d(h+u^2/2)/dx</math>. This is a reasonably good approximation since in normal gases, Pradntl number is approximately equal to <math>0.72</math>. With this approximation and integrating once more by imposing the condition that <math>h+u^2/2</math> is bounded downstream, we find<ref name="zeldo">Zel'Dovich, Y. B., & Raizer, Y. P. (2002). Physics of shock waves and high-temperature hydrodynamic phenomena. Courier Corporation.</ref>

<math display="block">h+\frac{u^2}{2} = h_0 +\frac{D^2}{2}.</math>

This above relation indicates that the quantity <math>h+u^2/2</math> is conserved everywhere, not just on the upstream and downstream side. Since for the polytropic gas <math>h=c_p T = \gamma p\upsilon/(\gamma-1)=c^2/(\gamma-1)</math>, where <math>\upsilon=1/\rho</math> is the [[specific volume]] and <math>c</math> is the [[sound speed]], the above equation provides the relation between the ratio <math>p(x)/p_0</math> and the corresponding velocity (or density or specific volume) ratio

<math display="block">\eta(x)=\frac{u}{D}=\frac{\rho_0}{\rho}=\frac{\upsilon}{\upsilon_0},</math>

i.e.,{{r|zeldo}}

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{p}{p_0} &= \frac{1}{\eta}\left[1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_0^2(1-\eta^2)\right] = \frac{\eta_1(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)-\eta^2}{\left[\eta_1(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)-1\right]\eta}, \\[1ex]
\eta_1 &= \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1} + \frac{2}{(\gamma+1)M_0^2},
\end{align}</math>

where <math>M_0=D/c_0</math> is the [[Mach number]] of the wave with respect to upstream and <math>\eta_1=u_1/D=\rho_0/\rho_1=\upsilon_1/\upsilon_0</math>. Combining this with momentum and continuity integrals, we obtain the equation for <math>\eta(x)</math> as follows

<math display="block">\frac{8\gamma}{3(\gamma+1)}\frac{\mu'}{\rho_0 D} \eta \frac{d\eta}{dx} = -(1-\eta)(\eta-\eta_1).</math>

We can introduce the reciprocal-viscosity-weighted coordinate<ref>Weiss, A. D., Vera, M., Liñán, A., Sánchez, A. L., & Williams, F. A. (2018). A novel formulation for unsteady counterflow flames using a thermal-conductivity-weighted coordinate. Combustion Theory and Modelling, 22(1), 185-201.</ref>

<math display="block">\xi = \frac{3(\gamma+1)}{8\gamma} \rho_0 D \int_0^x \frac{dt}{\mu'(t)}</math>

where <math>\mu'(x)=\mu'[T(x)]</math>, so that

<math display="block">\eta \frac{d\eta}{d\xi} = -(1-\eta)(\eta-\eta_1).</math>

The equation clearly exhibits the translation invariant in the <math>x</math>-direction which can be fixed, say, by fixing the origin to be the location where the intermediate value <math>(\eta_1+1)/2</math> is reached. Using this last condition, the solution to this equation is found to be{{r|zeldo}}

<math display="block">\frac{1-\eta}{(\eta-\eta_1)^{\eta_1}}= \left(\frac{1-\eta_1}{2}\right)^{1-\eta_1}e^{(1-\eta_1)\xi}.</math>

As <math>\xi\to-\infty</math> (or, <math>x\to-\infty</math>), we have <math>\eta\to 1</math> and as <math>\xi\to+\infty</math> (or, <math>x\to+\infty</math>), we have <math>\eta\to \eta_1.</math> This ends the search for the analytical solution. From here, other thermodynamics variables of interest can be evaluated. For instance, the temperature ratio <math>T/T_0</math> is  to found to given by

<math display="block">\frac{T}{T_0} = 1  + \frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_0^2 (1-\eta^2)</math>

and the [[specific entropy]] <math>s = c_p \ln (p^{1/\gamma}/\rho) = c_p\{\ln(p/\rho) - [(\gamma-1)/\gamma]\ln p\} </math>, by

<math display="block">\frac{s-s_0}{c_p} = \ln \frac{T}{T_0} - \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma} \ln \frac{p}{p_0}.</math>

The analytical solution is plotted in the figure for <math>\gamma=1.4</math> and <math>M_0=2</math>. The notable feature is that the entropy does not monotonically increase across the shock wave, but it increases to a larger value and then decreases to a constant behind the shock wave. Such scenario is possible because of the heat conduction, as it will become apparent by looking at the entropy equation which is obtained from the original energy equation by substituting the thermodynamic relation <math>Tds=d\varepsilon+pd\upsilon = dh-\rho^{-1}dp</math>, i.e.,

<math display="block">\rho u T \frac{ds}{dx} =  \frac{4}{3}\mu' \left(\frac{du}{dx}\right)^2 + \frac{d}{dx}\left(\lambda\frac{dT}{dx}\right).</math>

While the viscous dissipation associated with the term <math>(du/dx)^2</math> always increases the entropy, heat conduction increases the entropy in the colder layers where <math>d(\lambda dT/dx)/dx>0</math>, whereas it decreases the entropy in the hotter layers where <math>d(\lambda dT/dx)/dx<0</math>.

===Taylor's solution: Weak shock waves===
When <math>Pr'\neq 3/4</math>, analytical solution is possible only in the weak shock-wave limit, as first shown by [[G. I. Taylor]] in 1910.{{r|taylor}}  In the weak shock-wave limit, all terms such as <math>p-p_0</math>, <math>\rho-\rho_0</math> etc., will be small. The thickness <math>\delta</math>  of the shock wave is of the order <math>\delta \sim 1/(p_1-p_0)</math> so that differentiation with respect to <math>x</math> increases the order smallness by one; e.g. <math>dp/dx</math> is a second-order small quantity. Without going into the details and treating the gas to a generic gas (not just polytropic), the solution for <math>p(x)</math> is found to be related to the steady travelling-wave solution of the [[Burgers' equation#Steadily propagating traveling wave|Burgers' equation]] and is given by<ref>Landau, L. D., & Lifshitz, E. M. (2013). Fluid mechanics: Landau And Lifshitz: course of theoretical physics, Volume 6 (Vol. 6). Elsevier.</ref>

<math display="block">p(x) = \frac{1}{2}(p_1+p_0) + \frac{1}{2}(p_1-p_0) \tanh \frac{x}{\delta}</math>

where

<math display="block">\delta = \frac{8a\rho_0 c_0^4}{(p_1-p_0)\Gamma}, \quad a = \frac{\lambda_0}{2\rho_0 c_0^3c_p}\left(\frac{4}{3}Pr'+ \gamma-1\right),</math>

in which <math>\Gamma</math> is the [[Landau derivative]] (for polytropic gas <math>\Gamma=(\gamma+1)/2</math>) and <math>a</math> is a constant which when multiplied by some characteristic frequency squared provides the acoustic [[Attenuation coefficient|absorption coefficient]].<ref>Clavin, P., & Searby, G. (2016). Combustion waves and fronts in flows: flames, shocks, detonations, ablation fronts and explosion of stars. Cambridge University Press.</ref> The [[specific entropy]] is found to be proportional to <math>(1/T)dp/dx</math> and is given by

<math display="block">\frac{s(x) - s_0}{c_p} = \frac{\lambda_0 \Gamma}{8a c_p c_0T_0} \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial p}\right)_{s_0}\frac{(p_1-p_0)^2}{\rho_0^2c_0^4} \frac{1}{\cosh^2 (x/\delta)}.</math>

Note that <math>s(x)-s_0</math> is a second-order small quantity, although <math>s_1-s_0</math> is a third-order small quantity as can be inferred from the above expression which shows that <math>s=s_0</math> for both <math>x\to\pm\infty</math>. This is allowed since <math>s(x)</math>, unlike <math>p(x)</math>, passes through a maximum within the shock wave.

'''Validity of continuum hypothesis:''' since the [[thermal velocity]] of the molecules is of the order <math>c</math> and the kinematic viscosity is of the order <math>lc</math>, where <math>l</math> is the [[mean free path]] of the gas molecules,, we have <math>a\sim l/c^2</math>; an estimation based on heat conduction gives the same result. Combining this with the relation <math>p/\rho\sim c^2</math>, shows that

<math display="block">\delta \sim l,</math>

i.e., the shock-wave thickness is of the order the mean free path of the molecules. However, in the [[continuum hypothesis]], the mean free path is taken to be zero. It follows that the continuum equations alone cannot be strictly used to describe the internal structure of strong shock waves; in weak shock waves, <math>p_2-p_1</math> can be made as small as possible to make <math>\delta</math> large.

==Rayleigh's solution==
Two problems that were originally considered by [[Lord Rayleigh]] are given here.{{r|rayleigh}}

===Fluids with heat conduction and without viscosity (Pr&prime; &rarr; 0)===
The problem when viscosity is neglected but heat conduction is allowed is of significant interest in astrophysical context due to presence of other heat exchange mechanisms such as radiative heat transfer, electron heat transfer in [[Plasma (physics)|plasmas]], etc.{{r|zeldo}} Neglect of viscosity means viscous forces in the momentum equation and the viscous dissipation in the energy equation disappear. Hence the first integral of the governing equations are simply given by

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\rho u &= \rho_0 D,\\
p + \rho u^2  &= p_0 +\rho_0 D^2,\\
h + \frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{\lambda}{\rho_0 D}  \frac{dT}{dx} &=h_0 +\frac{D^2}{2}.
\end{align}
</math>

All the required ratios can be expressed in terms of <math>\eta</math> immediately,

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{p}{p_0} &= 1 + \gamma M_0^2(1-\eta),\\
\frac{T}{T_0} &= 1 +  (1-\eta) (\gamma M_0^2 \eta-1),\\
\frac{\lambda}{\rho_0 D^3}\frac{dT}{dx} & = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}(1-\eta)(\eta-\eta_1).
\end{align}</math>

By eliminating <math>\eta</math> from the last two equations, one can obtain equation <math>dT/dx=f(T)</math>, which can be integrated. It turns out there is no continuous solution for strong shock waves, precisely when{{r|zeldo}}

<math display="block">M_0^2 > \frac{3\gamma-1}{\gamma(3-\gamma)};</math>

for <math>\gamma=1.4</math> this condition becomes <math>M_0>1.2.</math>

===Fluids with viscosity and without heat conduction (Pr&prime; &rarr; &infin;)===

Here continuous solutions can be found for all shock wave strengths. Further, here the entropy increases monotonically across the shock wave due to the absence of heat conduction. Here the first integrals are given by

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\rho u &= \rho_0 D,\\
p + \rho u^2 - \frac{4}{3}\mu' \frac{du}{dx} &= p_0 +\rho_0 D^2,\\
h + \frac{u^2}{2} - \frac{4\mu'}{3\rho_0 D}   u\frac{du}{dx}&=h_0 +\frac{D^2}{2}.
\end{align}
</math>

One can eliminate the viscous terms in the last two equations and obtain a relation between <math>p/p_0</math> and <math>\eta</math>. Substituting this back in any one of the equations, we obtain an equation for <math>\eta(x)</math>, which can be integrated.
